reply:
Average transaction amount per customer: group Sales.CustomerTransactions by CustomerID and average TransactionAmount.

```sql
SELECT CustomerID, AVG(TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
GROUP BY CustomerID
ORDER BY CustomerID;
```

Customers link to a city through DeliveryCityID, and each city links to a state province through StateProvinceID. I join Customers to Cities to StateProvinces, then group by the state province name and count customers.

```sql
SELECT sp.StateProvinceName,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.StateProvinceName
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.StateProvinceName;
```

Quantity sold per stock item is best taken from the invoice lines (actual sales), averaged per stock item and joined to the stock item names. Using a LEFT JOIN keeps items that have no sales.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       AVG(il.Quantity) AS avg_quantity_sold
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
LEFT JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY si.StockItemID;
```

The question doesn't name a table, so I assumed the customer transactions table, `Sales.CustomerTransactions`. I also took "completed successfully" to mean a finalized transaction (`IsFinalized = true`). The query averages `TransactionAmount` over those rows.

```sql
SELECT AVG(TransactionAmount) AS average_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
WHERE IsFinalized = true;
```

Black Friday 2024 is Friday, 29 Nov 2024. I treated an order as "with promotion" if at least one of its lines matches a special deal that is active on that date. A deal matches when every target it specifies (stock item, customer, buying group, customer category, stock group) fits the line. Order value is the sum of `Quantity * UnitPrice` over the order's lines.

```sql
WITH line_flags AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice AS line_value,
           EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
               FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
               JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
               WHERE o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
                 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
                 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
                 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
                 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
                 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
                         SELECT 1
                         FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
                         WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
                           AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
           ) AS line_has_promo
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    WHERE o.OrderDate = DATE '2024-11-29'
),
order_values AS (
    SELECT OrderID,
           SUM(line_value) AS order_value,
           BOOL_OR(line_has_promo) AS has_promotion
    FROM line_flags
    GROUP BY OrderID
)
SELECT has_promotion,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       AVG(order_value) AS avg_order_value
FROM order_values
GROUP BY has_promotion
ORDER BY has_promotion DESC;
```

Account name here refers to the customer name, and "opened" corresponds to `AccountOpenedDate` in `Sales.Customers`. To get the earliest one and break ties by returning only one row, I order by that date ascending (with `CustomerID` as a deterministic tiebreaker) and limit to 1.

```sql
SELECT CustomerName
FROM Sales.Customers
ORDER BY AccountOpenedDate ASC, CustomerID ASC
LIMIT 1;
```

Backorders are recorded in Sales.Orders. An order that is itself a backorder has a non-null BackorderOrderID, and an order whose shortfall was backordered has IsUndersupplyBackordered = true.

In WideWorldImporters, BackorderOrderID on an original order points to the backorder that was created for it. So the customers who had backorders are those with at least one order where BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL. The backorder orders themselves belong to the same customers, so this filter covers them either way.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL;
```

Backorders are identified by Orders.BackorderOrderID being not null. Customers with backorders are counted per year by OrderDate, for 2000 to 2020. Years with no backorders won't show unless I generate them, so I'll use generate_series with a left join to include every year with a count of 0.

I'm counting distinct customers per year, based on the order date of the order that has a backorder.

```sql
SELECT y.year,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM generate_series(2000, 2020) AS y(year)
LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders o
       ON EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.OrderDate)::int = y.year
      AND o.BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY y.year
ORDER BY y.year;
```

Revenue is best measured from invoice lines: the sum of ExtendedPrice (which includes tax) or the sum of Quantity * UnitPrice (which excludes tax). Revenue usually means sales excluding tax, but ExtendedPrice is the standard invoiced amount in this schema. I'll use ExtendedPrice and join to invoices to filter on InvoiceDate between 2013-01-01 and 2013-03-31.

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2013-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2013-04-01';
```

The question doesn't say whether "stock count" means the number of stock items or the total quantity on hand. I read it as the number of stock items per brand, so the query counts rows in `Warehouse.StockItems`, skips items with no brand, and keeps the top 10. If you meant units on hand, you would instead sum `QuantityOnHand` from `Warehouse.StockItemHoldings`, joined on `StockItemID`.

```sql
SELECT Brand, COUNT(*) AS stock_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE Brand IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Brand
ORDER BY stock_count DESC, Brand
LIMIT 10;
```

Orders are in Sales.Orders, and OrderDate is a date column, so I filter it for 2013-11-01 exactly.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE OrderDate = DATE '2013-11-01'
ORDER BY OrderID;
```

Biggest consumer of the 'Northwind' brand: the customer with the highest total quantity purchased across invoice lines of stock items whose Brand is 'Northwind'.

Steps:
1. Join Sales.InvoiceLines to Warehouse.StockItems, filtering Brand = 'Northwind'.
2. Join to Sales.Invoices to get the CustomerID.
3. Join to Sales.Customers for the name.
4. Sum the quantity per customer, order descending, and take the top row.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
WHERE si.Brand = 'Northwind'
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Order value = sum of OrderLines Quantity * UnitPrice per order. Average these per order, grouped by the customer's category.

Steps:
1. Compute each order's total value from Sales.OrderLines (Quantity * UnitPrice).
2. Join to Sales.Orders, then Sales.Customers, then Sales.CustomerCategories.
3. Average the order totals per category.

```sql
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           o.CustomerID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    GROUP BY o.OrderID, o.CustomerID
)
SELECT cc.CustomerCategoryName,
       AVG(ot.order_value) AS average_order_value
FROM order_totals ot
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ot.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.CustomerCategories cc ON cc.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID
GROUP BY cc.CustomerCategoryName
ORDER BY average_order_value DESC;
```

Delay is the difference between the actual delivery time (Invoices.ConfirmedDeliveryTime) and the order's ExpectedDeliveryDate. I'll join Invoices to Orders, then to Customers to get the delivery city, and average the delay per city. Only invoices with a confirmed delivery time are included.

The delay is measured in days as `ConfirmedDeliveryTime - ExpectedDeliveryDate`. The average is used to rank cities, and the top 5 are returned.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName,
       AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime - o.ExpectedDeliveryDate::timestamp)) / 86400.0) AS avg_delay_days
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.OrderID = i.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers cu ON cu.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities c ON c.CityID = cu.DeliveryCityID
WHERE i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY avg_delay_days DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Ratio of salespeople to employees in Application.People: count of IsSalesperson divided by count of IsEmployee. I'll use numeric casting to avoid integer division, and NULLIF to guard against zero employees.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsSalesperson)::numeric / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsEmployee), 0) AS salesperson_to_employee_ratio
FROM Application.People;
```

The schema has no discount column on invoice or order lines, so I took "bought with discount" to mean customers with a standard discount (`StandardDiscountPercentage > 0`) who had at least one non-credit-note invoice dated in 2024. A line-level reading (invoice price below the stock item's list price) is also possible, but I went with the customer-level discount.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE c.StandardDiscountPercentage > 0
  AND i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2025-01-01'
  AND i.IsCreditNote = false;
```

The only vehicle-related data is in `Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures`, which stores a `VehicleRegistration` for each reading. Many readings can belong to the same vehicle, so counting rows would overcount. Counting distinct registrations gives the number of vehicles.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT VehicleRegistration) AS vehicle_count
FROM Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures;
```

Suppliers don't sell directly in this schema, so I treated "items sold" as the units sold on customer invoice lines for each supplier's stock items. The query joins `Sales.InvoiceLines` to `Warehouse.StockItems` to `Purchasing.Suppliers`, sums `Quantity` per supplier, and keeps the top 5. If you meant the number of distinct items instead, swap the sum for a count of distinct `StockItemID`.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = si.SupplierID
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_items_sold DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I made two assumptions.

- **"Items in stock":** I read this as every row in `Warehouse.StockItems`, not only items with `QuantityOnHand > 0` in `StockItemHoldings`.
- **"No tax rate attached":** `TaxRate` is declared `NOT NULL`, so a null check alone would always return 0. I treat a rate of 0 as "no tax rate", and keep the null check as a safeguard.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS items_without_tax_rate
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE TaxRate IS NULL OR TaxRate = 0;
```

Suppliers are linked to cities through DeliveryCityID, so I join Purchasing.Suppliers to Application.Cities on that column, group by city, count suppliers per city, and keep the top 5. I group by CityID as well as CityName, since different cities can share a name. Ties at the cutoff are broken by city name so the order is deterministic.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName, COUNT(*) AS supplier_count
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Application.Cities c ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY supplier_count DESC, c.CityName
LIMIT 5;
```

Stock items are in Warehouse.StockItems, which has both Size and UnitPrice. The query averages UnitPrice and groups by Size. Items with a NULL size fall into one group of their own, which is fine.

```sql
SELECT Size, AVG(UnitPrice) AS average_unit_price
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
GROUP BY Size;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I took "search terms" to mean the `Tags` column on `Warehouse.StockItems`. It holds a JSON array of keywords per item, such as `["Radio Control","Realistic sound"]`. The query expands each array into one row per tag, counts how many stock items carry each tag, and returns the six most frequent. Ties are broken alphabetically. I haven't run it against the database.

```sql
SELECT t.tag AS search_term,
       COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(
    CASE WHEN si.Tags IS NULL OR btrim(si.Tags) = '' THEN '[]'::jsonb ELSE si.Tags::jsonb END
) AS t(tag)
GROUP BY t.tag
ORDER BY item_count DESC, search_term
LIMIT 6;
```

Interpretation: "items ordered" means the total quantity of items across order lines, grouped by order date. I join Sales.Orders to Sales.OrderLines, sum the quantity per day, and take the day with the highest total.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderDate, SUM(ol.Quantity) AS total_items
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
GROUP BY o.OrderDate
ORDER BY total_items DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Interpretation: for each city that has suppliers (using the delivery city), compute population divided by the number of suppliers in it, then return the 5 highest ratios.

Steps:
1. Join Purchasing.Suppliers to Application.Cities on DeliveryCityID = CityID.
2. Group by city and count suppliers.
3. Compute LatestRecordedPopulation divided by the supplier count (cast to numeric to avoid integer division).
4. Order descending and limit to 5.

```sql
SELECT c.CityID,
       c.CityName,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation,
       COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS supplier_count,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation::numeric / COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS population_to_supplier_ratio
FROM Application.Cities c
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
WHERE c.LatestRecordedPopulation IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName, c.LatestRecordedPopulation
ORDER BY population_to_supplier_ratio DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "geographical area" as the sales territory and "targets" as the number of customers served there. Each customer's delivery city links to a state/province, which carries the `SalesTerritory`. I count customers per territory and keep the top 3.

```sql
SELECT sp.SalesTerritory,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.SalesTerritory
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.SalesTerritory
LIMIT 3;
```

The database has no direct link between invoices and special deals, so I matched them by each deal's conditions. An invoice line counts toward a deal if:

- the invoice date falls between the deal's start and end dates;
- the stock item, customer, buying group, customer category and stock group each match whenever the deal specifies them (a null on the deal means "any").

A deal's success is its total `ExtendedPrice` across the matching invoice lines, and the query returns the deal with the highest total. I haven't run this against the database.

```sql
SELECT sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_sales,
       SUM(il.LineProfit) AS total_profit,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
JOIN Sales.Invoices i
  ON i.InvoiceDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
JOIN Sales.Customers c
  ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il
  ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
WHERE (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR il.StockItemID = sd.StockItemID)
  AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR i.CustomerID = sd.CustomerID)
  AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR c.BuyingGroupID = sd.BuyingGroupID)
  AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR c.CustomerCategoryID = sd.CustomerCategoryID)
  AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sg
        WHERE sg.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
          AND sg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
GROUP BY sd.SpecialDealID, sd.DealDescription
ORDER BY total_sales DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

The question has no explicit table for regions, so I used `Application.Countries.Continent = 'North America'`. I linked each customer's delivery city to its state/province and then to its country. "Best sellers" is measured as total quantity sold from invoice lines, grouped by stock item. I did not run this query.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
JOIN Application.Countries co ON co.CountryID = sp.CountryID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE co.Continent = 'North America'
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC
LIMIT 4;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "sale transactions" as the rows in `Sales.CustomerTransactions`. The query groups them by calendar month (year and month together) and returns the month with the most rows. I did not filter by transaction type. If a tie matters, this returns only one of the tied months.

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', TransactionDate)::date AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS transaction_count
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', TransactionDate)
ORDER BY transaction_count DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Count orders per customer in Sales.Orders, keep those with more than 130 orders, and join to Sales.Customers for the name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
HAVING COUNT(o.OrderID) > 130
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

The question asks for the recorded temperatures in the cold room with timestamp and temperature values. The table Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures has RecordedWhen and Temperature columns, so I select those and order by time.

```sql
SELECT RecordedWhen, Temperature
FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures
ORDER BY RecordedWhen;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I used `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions` as the source of purchase amounts. I kept only rows tied to a purchase order, which are the supplier invoices (payments have no purchase order). I then summed `TransactionAmount` per supplier for 2014. An alternative would be to sum purchase order lines (ordered outers × expected unit price) by order date.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(st.TransactionAmount) AS total_purchases_2014
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
WHERE st.TransactionDate >= DATE '2014-01-01'
  AND st.TransactionDate < DATE '2015-01-01'
  AND st.PurchaseOrderID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_purchases_2014 DESC;
```

Orders link to customers via CustomerID, and customers link to buying groups via BuyingGroupID. I join Orders to Customers and then to BuyingGroups, and count the orders per group. An inner join to BuyingGroups leaves out customers who don't belong to any buying group, which fits "by each buying group".

```sql
SELECT bg.BuyingGroupID,
       bg.BuyingGroupName,
       COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.BuyingGroups bg
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.BuyingGroupID = bg.BuyingGroupID
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY bg.BuyingGroupID, bg.BuyingGroupName
ORDER BY bg.BuyingGroupID;
```

Invoices are in Sales.Invoices. InvoiceDate is a date column, so I filter with a half-open range covering May 2014 (from 2014-05-01 up to but not including 2014-06-01). I select the invoice id, customer id, and invoice date.

```sql
SELECT InvoiceID, CustomerID, InvoiceDate
FROM Sales.Invoices
WHERE InvoiceDate >= DATE '2014-05-01'
  AND InvoiceDate < DATE '2014-06-01'
ORDER BY InvoiceDate, InvoiceID;
```

Monthly summary: truncate the invoice date to the month, and sum the chiller and dry items. The question says "grouped by invoice date", but since it asks for a monthly summary, I group by month.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)::date AS invoice_month,
       SUM(TotalChillerItems) AS total_chiller_items,
       SUM(TotalDryItems) AS total_dry_items,
       SUM(TotalChillerItems + TotalDryItems) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.Invoices
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)
ORDER BY invoice_month;
```

The question asks for the total discount amount for each deal description, which comes straight from `Sales.SpecialDeals`. I group by `DealDescription` and sum `DiscountAmount`.

```sql
SELECT DealDescription, SUM(DiscountAmount) AS total_discount_amount
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals
GROUP BY DealDescription;
```

Interpreting "order details" as the order lines joined to their orders and customers, I join Sales.Orders to Sales.OrderLines and then to Sales.Customers to get the customer name.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       c.CustomerName,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.ExpectedDeliveryDate,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Sales.CustomerTransactions has a TransactionAmount column, which already includes tax (AmountExcludingTax + TaxAmount). Grouping by customer and averaging that column gives the average transaction amount including tax. I join to Sales.Customers so each row shows the customer's name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount_including_tax
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

Join the supplier transactions table to the suppliers table on SupplierID, so each transaction row carries its supplier's name.

```sql
SELECT st.*, s.SupplierName
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions AS st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers AS s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
ORDER BY st.SupplierTransactionID;
```

Approach: sum TransactionAmount per customer from Sales.CustomerTransactions, join to Sales.Customers for the name, order by the total descending, and limit to 100.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       SUM(ct.TransactionAmount) AS TotalTransactionAmount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions AS ct
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY TotalTransactionAmount DESC
LIMIT 100;
```

Order details here means the rows of Sales.OrderLines. Each row has a StockItemID, so I join it to Warehouse.StockItems to get the stock item name.

```sql
SELECT ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.OrderID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen,
       ol.LastEditedBy,
       ol.LastEditedWhen
FROM Sales.OrderLines AS ol
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems AS si ON si.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
ORDER BY ol.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "order details with special deals" as order lines that fall under a special deal. A line qualifies when the order date is within the deal's start and end dates and the deal's criteria match. A NULL criterion on a deal means it applies to everything:

- stock item
- stock group
- customer
- buying group
- customer category

I have not run the query against the database.

```sql
SELECT ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.OrderID,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.CustomerID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       sd.StartDate,
       sd.EndDate,
       sd.DiscountAmount,
       sd.DiscountPercentage,
       sd.UnitPrice AS DealUnitPrice
FROM Sales.OrderLines ol
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.OrderID = ol.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals sd
  ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sg
        WHERE sg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
          AND sg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
ORDER BY ol.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID, sd.SpecialDealID;
```
